channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: US GDP grew at an annualised 3.4% in the third quarter from 2.2% in the second, above forecasts of 3.1% to 3.2%, driven by AI-related business investment and consumer spending, which grew at a 3.8% pace.
item.description:
The Economic Times, The Standard and Les Echos report that the Bureau of Economic Analysis put US gross domestic product growth in the third quarter at an annualised 3.4%; Les Echos adds that this is up from 2.2% in the previous quarter and the highest in a year. The Economic Times gives a Reuters poll forecast of 3.2% and Les Echos a Bloomberg median of 3.2%, while Nihon Keizai Shimbun cites a Dow Jones forecast of 3.1%. The Standard says consumer spending, more than two thirds of the economy, grew at a 3.8% pace. The rows credit AI-related business investment and resilient consumer spending, which offset the effect of higher oil prices tied to the Middle East conflict. The Economic Times says the pace is well above the roughly 2% some Federal Reserve officials regard as the non-inflationary rate. The Globe and Mail reports that the personal consumption expenditures price index rose 0.5% in September, in line with expectations, and core PCE inflation was 3.1% year on year. The rows do not give the split of growth between investment and consumption in comparable terms, trade or inventory effects, or a revision schedule.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report one quarter of growth and a monthly inflation figure, not a forecast. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, growth well above the roughly 2% pace that some Federal Reserve officials regard as non-inflationary, together with core PCE inflation of 3.1% year on year, makes lower interest rates less likely, and a boom in investment tied to one sector can leave other sectors out. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, US manufacturing and construction customers use bonding, sealing and coating materials, so strong demand could support orders, while higher interest rates could dampen housing and equipment investment, and the rows give no figures for either. Points that may be worth considering include the next Federal Reserve meeting, US construction and housing data, and the spread of growth beyond AI-related sectors.

The Economic Times | The Standard | Les Echos | Nihon Keizai Shimbun | The Globe and Mail

item.title: The ECB held its deposit rate at 2.5% on 29 October without signalling further tightening, the euro fell to a 17-month low of 1.1103 dollars, and President Christine Lagarde said she will leave on 7 February, nine months early.
item.description:
Commercial Times reports that the ECB kept the deposit rate at 2.5% and the refinancing and marginal lending rates at 2.65% and 2.9%, gave no signal of further tightening, and that the euro fell from 1.1131 to 1.1103 dollars, a 17-month low. The Economic Times adds that the ECB pointed to rising inflation risks linked to energy prices, that the euro hit an 18-month low against the pound, and that euro-area bond yields eased slightly. The FAZ reports that Lagarde will step down on 7 February, and Fortune says she is to step down nine months before the end of her term, which opens the way for European leaders to choose a successor ahead of France's presidential election next year. Fortune adds that chief economist Philip Lane's term ends on 31 May and Isabel Schnabel resigns on 3 January to join the International Monetary Fund, leaving three vacancies that European leaders are expected to apportion in a package deal. Cnyes wrote before the decision that euro-area inflation is close to 4%, mainly in energy, and that the French government bond market is volatile. Le Dauphine Libere reports that the French 10-year yield crossed 5% on 21 October, the first time since 2002, with a record gap to Germany, and that Julie Bachet, managing director of Vousfinancer, expects further rate increases, with average 20-year mortgage rates that could approach 4% by the end of 2026 and even 4.5% by the 2027 presidential election. The rows do not give the ECB's statement, projections, a vote, candidates for the succession or yields after the decision.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report a rate hold, a leadership change and a bond-market signal, not a change in rates. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, unchanged policy rates with inflation near 4% keep financing costs high, a weaker euro raises the price of imports invoiced in dollars such as oil, and a succession contest can add uncertainty about the rate path. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, construction and manufacturing customers in the euro area time projects and investment with financing costs in mind, so higher mortgage and loan rates could slow orders for bonding, sealing and coating materials, and the rows give no figures for either. Points that may be worth considering include the December ECB meeting, the French bond yield and mortgage rates, and the choice of Lagarde's successor.

Commercial Times | The Economic Times | Fortune | Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung | Cnyes | Le Dauphiné Libéré

item.title: Russia will extend its diesel export ban to the end of the year while letting some companies export under quotas to meet its commitment to the US, two people familiar with the discussions told Reuters, The Moscow Times reports.
item.description:
The Moscow Times reports, citing two people familiar with the discussions who spoke to Reuters, that Russia will extend its diesel export ban until the end of the year and allow some companies to ship fuel under a quota system to meet its new export commitment to the United States. Moscow and Washington agreed a diesel supply deal after Presidents Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump spoke by phone earlier in October. The energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, announced alongside the agreement, has allowed Moscow to raise fuel production, while fuel shortages earlier in 2026 led the government to keep tight control over oil product exports. Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said on Tuesday that three tankers with Russian diesel were already under way to export markets and that a fourth would sail on 28 October. This is one source and rests on anonymous people. The row does not give the quota size, the companies, the destinations, the volume to be sent to the US or any price effect.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports a plan from anonymous sources and a statement by a minister, not a published decree. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a ban with quotas limits exports to the volumes set for specific deals, so diesel supply to other buyers depends on how the quotas are allocated. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, diesel is a transport fuel, so supply and price changes could reach freight and logistics costs for chemical raw materials and finished products, and the row gives no figures. Points that may be worth considering include the text of any decree, the size of the quota, and diesel prices in Europe.

The Moscow Times

item.title: The US Federal Communications Commission voted on 29 October to bar test labs in countries that deny US labs reciprocal treatment, including China, from testing electronics such as computers, smartphones and cameras, from December 2028.
item.description:
The Express Tribune reports that on 29 October the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) voted to prohibit certification bodies and test labs in countries including China that deny reciprocal treatment to US-based test labs from testing electronic devices such as computers, smartphones and cameras for use in the US. According to FCC Chair Brendan Carr, 82% of electronics were tested in China in 2025; the row adds that China does not have an agreement with the US. The prohibitions are set to take effect in December 2028. The FCC also streamlined the approval process for devices tested in US labs or in labs in countries that do not pose national security risks. This is one source. The row does not give the list of countries covered, the number of labs, the value of the devices concerned, the cost to manufacturers, a Chinese response or the vote count.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports a vote with an effective date more than two years away, not a change in trade flows. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a rule that moves testing away from China adds time and cost to product certification and can move testing capacity to other countries, and the long lead time leaves room for changes. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, computers, smartphones and cameras are assembled with bonding, sealing and coating materials, so a shift in where devices are tested may change development timelines for electronics customers, and the row gives no figures for materials. Points that may be worth considering include the FCC's list of countries, the response of China, and testing capacity in the US and other countries.

The Express Tribune

item.title: China's Commerce Ministry said on 29 October it will take "all necessary measures" if the EU imposes discriminatory restrictions, after media reports that the EU is considering extending its hybrid-car trade understanding to chemicals.
item.description:
China Economic Net, China Daily, People's Daily Online and Bjd.com.cn report that on 29 October Huang Ling, a spokeswoman for China's Commerce Ministry, responded to media reports that the EU is considering extending the trade understanding on hybrid vehicles, reached with China, to chemicals and other fields. She said artificial restrictions on normal trade are suspected of violating World Trade Organization rules, would not improve the competitiveness of EU industries, would burden downstream industries, push up EU inflation and affect the stability of global industrial and supply chains. If the EU persists with discriminatory restrictions on Chinese products, China will take all necessary measures to defend its interests. Bjd.com.cn adds that China is willing to continue dialogue and opposes any protectionist misuse of trade defence tools. Global Times says EU trade ministers discussed possible measures involving chemicals and machinery on 23 October. The Nation describes the hybrid understanding, reached in Beijing on 8–9 October, as principles of non-discrimination, WTO compliance and continued growth from the 2025 import baseline. The rows do not name the outlets behind the media reports, the chemicals or instruments considered, any dates or rates, or an EU position.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report a Chinese statement about a reported EU option, not an EU measure. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, trade measures on chemicals would change the landed price of the products named and move buying between origins, and a threat of countermeasures widens the range of goods that could be affected. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, chemicals are raw materials, so a change in supply or price of Chinese chemical inputs, or Chinese measures on EU chemical exports, could reach production costs and sourcing in Europe, and the rows give no figures for products or trade values. Points that may be worth considering include the list of chemicals and instruments the EU discusses after the 23 October ministers' meeting, the form of any Chinese response, and the treatment of downstream products.

China Economic Net | China Daily | People's Daily Online | Bjd.com.cn | Global Times | The Nation

item.title: The Taiwan Semiconductor Industry Association's chairman said on 29 October that Taiwan's semiconductor output value is expected to rise 40.9% in 2026 to more than TWD 9.1 trillion; one row gives the TWD 6.5 trillion 2025 base as members' output.
item.description:
Chinatimes and Commercial Times report that the chairman of the Taiwan Semiconductor Industry Association (TSIA), who is also a senior executive at TSMC, announced at the association's 30th anniversary annual meeting on 29 October that the industry's output value is projected to exceed TWD 9.1 trillion in 2026, 40.9% more than in 2025. Chinatimes says the 2025 level of TWD 6.5 trillion refers to the output of TSIA's members, while Commercial Times gives it as the output value of the industry. The figures are a projection announced by the association's chairman. The rows do not give the reasons for the rise, a split by product or customer, capital spending plans, the currency effect or other forecasts for the industry.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report a projection from the industry's own association. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, an output value projection combines volume, prices and mix, so it cannot be read as a unit forecast, and the base of members compared with the whole industry matters. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, semiconductors and electronic assemblies use bonding, sealing and coating materials in chip packaging and in the devices they go into, so higher output could support demand from electronics customers in Taiwan, and the rows give no figures for materials. Points that may be worth considering include the association's capital spending data, monthly export figures for semiconductors, and demand from device makers.

Chinatimes | Commercial Times

item.title: Margins of Indian small manufacturers that make finished goods from polymers have halved since the West Asia war began on 28 February, LiveMint reports, with industry bodies calling September a turning point as many firms ran out of cash buffers.
item.description:
LiveMint reports that since the West Asia war began on 28 February, the margins of micro, small and medium enterprises in India that use polymers to make finished products have halved, while higher prices of the crude oil from which polymers are made have strained their working capital. According to industry bodies, September was a turning point because many of these firms ran out of cash buffers and could not pass the full increase in costs on to customers. Many that export finished goods face order cancellations because of the war. A rise in shipping costs adds to the pressure by raising the cost of both raw material imports and finished-product exports. This is one source. The row does not give the margin levels before or after, the polymers or products concerned, the number of firms, the size of the cost increase or the freight rates.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row describes squeezed margins at small converters, reported by industry bodies, not a price series. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, converters that cannot pass costs on tend to cut orders, delay payments or stop buying when cash runs short, and their buying behaviour reaches suppliers early. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, polymer processors and finished-goods makers use bonding, sealing and coating materials in production and packaging, so weaker cash positions among them could affect order sizes and payment terms in India, and the same oil-linked cost rise applies to the raw materials of the industry itself, while the row gives no figures. Points that may be worth considering include polymer price data for India, payment delays among small customers, and export order trends.

LiveMint

item.title: Japan's industrial output rose 2.2% in September from August after a revised 2.4% fall, led by motor vehicles up 5.5% as plants recovered from typhoon and earthquake shutdowns, and production machinery up 3.4% on chip-equipment exports.
item.description:
The Mainichi reports government data showing that industrial output in Japan rose 2.2% in September from the previous month, after a downwardly revised fall of 2.4% in August, the first increase in three months. The seasonally adjusted index stood at 104.1 against 100 in 2020. Output rose in eight of 15 sectors, led by motor vehicles, up 5.5% as passenger vehicle production returned to normal after plant shutdowns caused by typhoons and the magnitude-7.1 earthquake that hit Kumamoto Prefecture on 28 July. Production machinery rose 3.4% on higher exports of semiconductor manufacturing equipment to Taiwan, China and South Korea, and general-purpose and business-oriented machinery rose 4.8%. Output fell in seven sectors, including iron, steel and non-ferrous metals, down 1.6% partly because of regular plant repairs that cut galvanised steel sheet output, and ceramics, stone and clay products, down 1.9% because of equipment problems in glass fibre production. This is one source. The row does not give the year-on-year change, vehicle unit numbers or a forecast for October.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports a month-on-month rebound from disruption, not a trend in demand. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a recovery after shutdowns shows capacity restarting, and the level of output compared with before the disruption says more about demand than the monthly change. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, motor vehicles and production machinery are customers for bonding, sealing and coating materials, so the restart of vehicle plants could have supported demand from Japanese automotive customers in September, while the fall in glass fibre output may have affected composite producers, and the row gives no figures for materials. Points that may be worth considering include the October output data, the level of vehicle production compared with July, and exports of chip-making equipment.

The Mainichi

item.title: President Trump announced at a Georgia rally that Audi plans to invest about USD 4 billion in a new US factory, and German politicians and union leaders criticise Audi's chief executive for appearing with him, LiveMint reports.
item.description:
LiveMint reports that Audi's chief executive Gernot Döllner is criticised by German politicians and trade union leaders after he appeared alongside President Trump at a campaign rally in Georgia, where Trump announced the carmaker's plan to invest around USD 4 billion in a new US factory. The row says the investment is intended to expand Audi's presence in the North American market. It says Trump promotes tariffs as a way to encourage companies to build more vehicles in the US, and that German manufacturers have warned that trade barriers raise costs and complicate investment decisions. This is one source, and the announcement came from the US President, not from a company statement quoted in the row. The row does not give the location in Georgia, capacity, start date, models, jobs, the timing of the spending, whether it is new or part of earlier plans, or the objections raised by the critics.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports an announced plan, not a decision with a schedule. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a new US plant by a German carmaker moves part of the value added from German and European plants to the US and favours suppliers that can serve it locally. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, a new vehicle plant uses bonding, sealing and coating materials in assembly, so a US plant could create demand from US operations of material suppliers, while German plants may see less, and the row gives no figures. Points that may be worth considering include Audi's own statement, the production start and model plan, and similar announcements by other German carmakers.

LiveMint

item.title: Toyota's April–September global sales fell 4.0% to 5.06 million, its first first-half drop in two years; September sales in China fell 27–62% at Honda, Nissan and Toyota, and the retail share of Japanese brands there has declined to 10.7%.
item.description:
The Mainichi reports that Toyota, the world's largest automaker by sales volume, posted its first fiscal first-half declines in global sales and production in two years amid weaker demand in China: sales including Lexus fell 4.0% to 5,059,014 units and production fell 1.9% to 4,895,406. The eight Japanese automakers sold a combined 11.83 million vehicles worldwide, down 1.3%, and Suzuki overtook Honda for second place among Japanese automakers with a record 1,824,006 units, up 19.9%, amid stronger sales in India, where it holds a 40% share of the passenger car market. Commercial Times reports that Toyota's global September sales, excluding Hino and Daihatsu, fell 2.2% to 860,107 units, the third monthly decline in a row, while electric vehicle sales doubled to a monthly record. China Economic Net reports that September sales in China of Honda, Nissan and Toyota fell by 53.1%, 61.6% and 26.9% year on year, that the retail share of Japanese brands has fallen to 10.7%, and gives the lag in new-energy vehicles as the main reason. The rows do not give sales volumes in China, the share a year earlier, whether the China figures are wholesale or retail, or an outlook.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows describe falling sales for Japanese brands in China, with higher sales for Suzuki in India. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a shift of sales between brands changes which assembly plants and supplier networks carry the volume, and the mix of electric and combustion models changes the materials in each vehicle. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, vehicle bodies, glass, interiors and battery packs are bonded, sealed and coated in assembly, so lower sales for Japanese brands in China and higher sales for Suzuki in India could move demand between plants and suppliers, and the rows give no figures for materials. Points that may be worth considering include the October sales figures, the sales of Chinese brands in China, and the electric share of Toyota's sales.

The Mainichi | China Economic Net | Commercial Times

item.title: Far East spot prices for ethylene and propylene rose by USD 40 each and benzene by USD 19 in a catch-up as oil passed USD 115, and five general-purpose resins rose USD 15 to USD 85, Commercial Times reports.
item.description:
Commercial Times reports that Far East petrochemical spot prices showed strong catch-up gains as oil broke USD 115 amid the Middle East conflict. Ethylene and propylene each rose by USD 40 and benzene rebounded by USD 19, and SM, PTA and EG followed with rises of USD 43, USD 52 and USD 40. Spot prices of the five major general-purpose resins also started a catch-up rally, which the row attributes to rising costs and to India's proposed anti-subsidy duties on mainland China: PE rose USD 40 to USD 85, PS USD 70, ABS USD 45, PP USD 30 and PVC USD 15. The row lists producers, by stock code, that it says benefit. This is one source. The row does not state the unit of the price changes, the period over which they occurred, which oil benchmark passed USD 115, or the price levels before the rises, and it does not say whether the rises reached contract prices.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports spot quotations in the Far East, not contract prices or volumes. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a rally that starts with monomers usually reaches resin prices and then converters' costs with a lag, and Asian spot prices need not match contract prices in Europe. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, monomers and polymers are raw materials for bonding, sealing and coating products, so a sustained rise could reach input costs with a delay and could lift prices of films and plastic parts made from these resins, and the row gives no figures for either. Points that may be worth considering include whether oil stays above USD 115, the move in European contract prices for the same products, and the outcome of India's proposed duties.

Commercial Times
